idiom_name: struct with a function-pointer slot, an inverse slot and an explicit void *context
implementation_notes: C has neither closures nor objects, so the whole structure is written by hand: a command is a struct holding a function pointer for the operation, a second pointer for its inverse when undo is required, and a void *context that the callee casts back to the receiver. That is the calling convention the standard library already uses for callbacks - qsort takes int (*comp)(const void *, const void *) and C11's qsort_s adds an explicit void *context parameter precisely because a callback carries no captured state. The invoker is an array of such structs plus an index; there is no idiom that replaces the class hierarchy here, only a disciplined naming convention plus factory functions that keep the context type honest.
pitfalls: Type erasure through void * removes every type check: build commands through per-command factory functions so the context pointer always refers to the receiver type the callbacks expect.
With no closures the captured context must outlive the command - a struct built over a stack frame or a freed object becomes a dangling pointer the moment the invoker runs it.
Undo has no state capture to fall back on, so the inverse callback must encode the exact prior value (position and deleted text) at creation time rather than reconstructing it later.
A fixed history array silently overflows; the invoker must bound and drop entries explicitly, since nothing in the language will do it.
